tagline: Island of Aphrodite, divided by a line
overview:
Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, lying in its far eastern corner, closer to Turkey, Syria, and Lebanon than to mainland Europe. It is about the size of Connecticut. Golden beaches ring the coast, and two mountain ranges rise inland, with the capital, Nicosia, on the dusty plain between them. Ancient Greeks believed Aphrodite, the goddess of love, was born from the sea foam off its southwestern shore.

Around 1.3 million people live on the island. Greek and Turkish are the official languages, reflecting its two main communities. Since 1974 Cyprus has been divided: the Republic of Cyprus, which joined the European Union in 2004, governs the south, while the northern third is run by a Turkish Cypriot administration recognized only by Turkey. A United Nations buffer zone, the Green Line, runs between them and cuts right through Nicosia, making it the last divided capital in Europe. Tourism, shipping, and services drive the economy, and Cypriots enjoy one of the sunniest climates in Europe.
landAndNature: The Troodos Mountains fill the center and southwest of the island, topped by Mount Olympus at 1,952 meters, high enough for a short ski season in winter while people swim on the coast below. Their forests of black pine and golden oak hide tiny painted churches from the Middle Ages. Along the north coast runs the long, narrow Kyrenia range of jagged limestone. Between the ranges the Mesaoria plain grows wheat, olives, and carob. Summers are hot and dry, winters mild and wet. The Cyprus mouflon, a wild sheep with huge curled horns, lives only in the Paphos forest. Green and loggerhead turtles nest on beaches like Lara Bay, and salt lakes near Larnaca and Akrotiri fill each winter with thousands of pink flamingos.
peopleAndCulture: Greek Cypriots, mostly Orthodox Christian, make up the majority, and Turkish Cypriots, mostly Muslim, live largely in the north; both communities share a love of coffee, backgammon, and long family lunches. Halloumi, a squeaky white cheese that can be grilled without melting, is the island's most famous food, joined by souvlaki, sheftalia sausages, and meze, a parade of dozens of small dishes. Commandaria, a sweet wine, may be the oldest named wine still made, dating back at least 800 years. Easter is the biggest holiday in the south, with fireworks and roasted lamb, while Ramadan and Bayram are celebrated in the north. Soccer is the most popular sport, and Cypriot villages keep lace-making and pottery traditions alive.
history: People have lived on Cyprus for about 10,000 years, and the island's copper mines were so famous that its name and the word copper may share a root. Greeks settled around 1200 BC, followed by rule under Assyrians, Egyptians, Persians, Alexander the Great, Romans, Byzantines, Crusaders, Venetians, and, from 1571, the Ottoman Empire. Britain took control in 1878 and made it a colony. Cyprus became independent in 1960, but tension between Greek and Turkish Cypriots led to violence. In 1974 a coup backed by Greece's military government was followed by a Turkish invasion, and the island was split, with about 200,000 people displaced from their homes. Talks to reunite the island have continued for decades. The Republic of Cyprus joined the EU in 2004.
funFacts: Nicosia is the only capital city in Europe still divided by a barrier, with checkpoints in the middle of its old town.
A Cypriot village called Lefkara made lace so fine that, according to tradition, Leonardo da Vinci bought a piece for Milan's cathedral.
Cyprus has no natural lakes; its salt lakes fill only with winter rain and dry to white crusts in summer.
The Cyprus mouflon appears on the country's coins and was once hunted almost to extinction.
Cypriots consume more halloumi per person than anyone else, and the cheese has protected status in the European Union.
